one_liner: Go event-loop networking library serving net/http handlers; beats Sogou workflow (C++) on HTTP/1 echo, ties uSockets on TLS.
what_it_does: fib is an event-driven networking engine for Go covering TCP, UDP, Unix sockets, TLS, HTTP/1.x, HTTP/2 (h2 and h2c), HTTP/3 over its own QUIC, WebSocket, arpc and gRPC. HTTP handlers receive a standard *http.Request and answer through a Context that implements http.ResponseWriter, so net/http handlers, http.ServeMux, chi or gin engines can be served on it with the caveats below; it also has a chi-style Router, middleware and a raw-TCP callback API (fib.Bind with Data callbacks). It is a Go library, not a replacement for a C or C++ server binary.
how_it_is_fast: A few event loops only wait for readiness (edge-triggered epoll, kqueue, IOCP) and hand ready connections in one batch to a P-sharded, lock-free (Vyukov MPMC ring) worker pool, so an idle connection holds no goroutine and no I/O buffer. A worker reads until a short read, runs the parser and handler, and corks every response of the round into one writev or sendfile, which is where the pipelining numbers come from; on Linux sockets are read and written with raw recvfrom/sendto/sendmsg system calls. After the crypto/tls handshake fib runs the AES-GCM and AES-CBC record layers itself and decrypts in place, and request, header, URL and Context objects are recycled fasthttp-style to keep the Go heap and GC out of the hot path.
when_to_use: Go servers holding many mostly idle connections (WebSocket, long polling, device gateways): no goroutine per idle connection; 32 MB at 10,000 WebSocket connections vs 229 MB for gorilla in the author's run.
Existing net/http handlers that need more HTTP/1.1 throughput, especially pipelined: 2.3x net/http on echo and 6.9x on pipelining in the author's go-http1-benchmark run.

One Go engine serving HTTP/1.1, h2, h2c, HTTP/3 and gRPC: in HttpArena fib is ahead of nginx on baseline-h2-256 (1.65x), baseline-h2c-256 (5.25x), baseline-h3-64 (1.25x) and static-tls-1024 (1.71x), ratios derived from page data.

TLS-terminating Go services on AES-GCM where crypto/tls over net costs throughput or memory: 2.3-2.9x crypto/tls pipelining on about a third of the memory, and a tie with uSockets plus BoringSSL on TLS 1.3 echo.
when_not_to_use: Anything you need to copy or vendor: the repository has no LICENSE file (raw LICENSE returns 404, the repo page shows no license), so by default no reuse rights are granted.

Production-critical services today: on 2026-10-11 (issue #1) the author wrote that it has not yet been heavily used in production, that client-side work is still in progress, and advised starting with small features; 27 stars, no tagged releases on the repo page.

Handlers that block (synchronous database calls, long waits) or keep request objects after returning: handlers run on scarce engine workers, and recycled Request/Header/URL/Context objects are handed to the next request once the handler returns.

Peak throughput against the best C and C++ servers: in HttpArena it trails nginx on baseline-4096 (0.96x), json-tls-4096 (774,182 vs 1,313,755) and json-h2c-1024 (1,102,054 vs 1,730,838), agensio (C++) by 2.6x on baseline-h2-256 and 2.2x on json-tls, libreactorng (C) by 2.1x on pipelined-4096 and mongoose on most WebSocket profiles.
Tight memory budgets: workflow serves the same HTTP/1 echo in 14 MB vs fib's 32 MB, and uSockets the TLS runs in 51 MB vs 180 MB.

integration.dependencies: none outside the Go standard library (README); gRPC with google.golang.org/protobuf messages needs a codec registered with grpc.RegisterCodec
integration.platforms: Linux (epoll, raw socket syscalls, prefork), macOS (kqueue), Windows (IOCP) on amd64, arm64, 386, arm, riscv64 and loong64; FreeBSD and other systems fall back to the standard net package
integration.thread_safety: Each connection's events run one at a time, in FIFO order, on whichever worker is idle; handlers share the engine's worker pool (HTTP/2, HTTP/3, async arpc and gRPC handlers run on a separate streams pool). Recycled request objects belong to a handler only until it returns and releases every Retain; keep copies (Request.Clone, Header.Clone) for anything used later.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — net/http handlers run on it unchanged within the documented limits, but it does not replace workflow, uSockets or nginx deployments, and it is a Go library rather than a C or C++ server

gotchas: Object reuse is on by default under fasthttp's RequestCtx rule: a net/http handler that keeps the *http.Request, its Header or URL past its return (for example in a goroutine started without Retain) reads or writes another request's data. http.Hijacker is not implemented, so gorilla/websocket does not work, and Request.Context() is not cancelled when the client goes away.

Writes never block and request bodies are buffered whole by default: a handler that writes faster than the peer reads queues the difference in memory (reads pause at a 64 KiB watermark, MaxPendingBytes is off by default), and over TLS SendFile reads and encrypts the whole range up front.

The HttpArena numbers run under prefork: a child process per two CPUs (GOMAXPROCS=2 each, so 32 processes on 64 cores) sharing ports with SO_REUSEPORT; the docs say one process with 64 Ps stalls on Go's shared heap lock and GC (baseline 1.23M to 1.63M req/s only after object reuse). Children share nothing but the port, so in-memory state exists once per child and HTTP/3 datagrams after a NAT rebinding can reach a child without the connection.

Harness limits of the headline numbers: go-*-benchmark rows are single runs on a shared 4-vCPU GitHub runner whose run annotation says the container got 4 CPUs instead of the 8 it wants, with client and server on the same VM; workflow ran its stock benchmark server (2 pollers plus 20 handler threads on 2 vCPUs, Date formatted with strftime on every response vs fib's once-a-second cached Date) and has no pipeline row because it closes connections on pipelined input; the TLS pipeline rows (690,000, 735,000, 750,000) come from a rate-driven phase that measures how much of the offered rate each server held. HttpArena rows are cross-run (fib.json saved 2026-10-08 by the fib author, nginx.json 2026-08-30).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick fib over nilo (baseline-h2c-256 9,010,310 vs fib 12,891,491) or Helidon SE (baseline-h2-256 3,612,898 vs 5,634,126) when you want a Go codebase with net/http-style handlers and HTTP/1.1, h2, h2c, HTTP/3, WebSocket and gRPC on one engine; for raw HTTP/1.1 throughput the HttpArena siblings zix, zeemo, vanilla and minima-sync (4.3-4.4M req/s on baseline-4096 vs fib's 3.16M) are faster, and tokio-websockets ties it on echo-ws-limited-4096 (2,641,801 vs 2,613,729).
verified_claims_summary: In the author's go-http1-benchmark (one GitHub Actions run, ubuntu-24.04 runner with 4 vCPUs split 2/2 between server and Rust tokio client, 10,000 connections, 1 KiB POST echo), fib at commit 4ffe768 built with Go 1.27 completed 194,671 round trips/s against Sogou workflow v1.1.0 (C++, Release build, server at -O3) at 150,407 (1.29x), using 32 MB vs 14 MB; in go-tls-benchmark against uSockets with BoringSSL (C) it tied on TLS 1.3 echo (103,427 vs 103,972) and reached 0.94x on TLS 1.3 pipelining. In HttpArena (Threadripper PRO 3995WX per site/data/current.json, separate runs) it trails nginx 1.31.4 on baseline-4096 (3,164,504 vs 3,284,513) and leads it on HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and static TLS profiles, where agensio (C++) is ahead of fib on the HTTP/2 rows.
status_note: Actively developed (last commit 2026-10-11, 297 commits, 27 stars, no tagged releases on the repo page) and, by the author's own account, not yet proven in heavy production use; with no LICENSE file it stays reference-only. No correctness bug was found behind the measured numbers (the hand-written TLS CBC record check copies crypto/tls's constant-time padding logic), but the first-party rows are single runs with the harness limits listed under gotchas. HttpArena's machine model is in site/data/current.json (Threadripper PRO 3995WX) and fib's Go build flags are in frameworks/fib/Dockerfile, so its HttpArena wins over nginx (h2c 5.25x, h2 1.65x, h3 1.25x, static-tls 1.71x, pipelined 5.05x, derived from page data) meet the same basis on which dusty, wtx and cutelyst were tiered A, subject to the cross-run and agensio caveats.
